Education: Integrating Simulated User Feedback for

Abstract—This study presents CancerSB, a serious adventure
game developed to raise awareness about bone cancer through an
engaging, point-and-click experience. Players explore culturally
themed levels—Chile, Italy, and China—each symbolizing bone
regions affected by cancer, solving puzzles, collecting items, and
simulating treatment decisions. The game integrates original
art, narrative, and educational content, and was developed with
medical input to ensure accurate bone cancer representation.
To evaluate early design choices, we used ChatGPT to generate
simulated feedback from diverse user personas, following the
“mega-personas” approach. Results suggest consistent positive
reception across personas, particularly for visual design, cultural
sensitivity, and educational value. These findings serve as a pre-
liminary validation and demonstrate the value of this approach
for guiding design improvements prior to user testing.
Index Terms—serious games, educational, health, bone cancer,
simulated user feedback
I. INTRODUCTION
Bone cancer, characterized by the abnormal growth of cells
in bones, can be influenced by hereditary factors, environ-
mental exposures, and individual risk factors According to the
American Cancer Society [1], projections for primary bone and
joint cancers in 2024 estimate approximately 3,970 new cases
(2,270 in men and 1,700 in women) and 2,050 deaths (1,100
in men and 950 in women). These figures encompass bone
cancers in both children and adults. Although primary bone
cancers account for less than 1% of all cancer cases, metastatic
bone cancers—originating from other organs—are far more
common in adults. These statistics emphasize the importance
of raising awareness and providing educational resources to
aid early detection and effective treatment.
Global epidemiological data reveal that bone cancer pri-
marily affects adolescents and young adults aged 15–24, with

Osteosarcoma showing a notable male predominance (male-to-
female ratio of 1.4:1) [2]. Although rare, primary bone cancers
have global age-standardized incidence rates of 0.8–1.2 per
100,000 person-years. The overall five-year survival rate is
around 66%, but drops to 27–58% in metastatic cases. A cross-
national study in 29 countries found that diagnosis delays over
three months increase mortality risk by 33%, emphasizing the
need for earlier detection and improved treatment strategies.
Despite its relatively lower prevalence compared to other
cancer types, the significant impact of bone cancer warrants
the necessity of developing innovative educational tools and
awareness campaigns. However, the field of health education
and training lacks engaging resources, such as serious games
and simulators, that specifically address bone cancer. Most
existing educational materials focus on more prevalent cancers,
such as breast, lung, and prostate cancer, highlighting the need
for targeted educational tools addressing less common cancers.
This work is part of a broader research initiative focused
on developing serious games for cancer diagnosis, treatment,
and awareness. It introduces CancerSB, a serious adventure
game designed to raise awareness about bone cancer through
an engaging point-and-click puzzle experience. Players explore
regions like Chile, Italy, and China—each symbolizing parts of
the body affected by different bone cancers—by solving chal-
lenges, collecting items, and simulating treatment decisions.
Developed with input from oncology professionals, the game
integrates original art, design, and animations with game-based
learning to offer an immersive educational experience. To
support development, we conducted a preliminary validation
using simulated user feedback. Following the “mega-personas”
approach by Steinmacher et al. [3], we used ChatGPT 4o to
simulate feedback from diverse user profiles, enabling early-
stage evaluation of our serious game. Grounded in recent
advances in large language models [4], this method allowed

us to explore how different types of users might perceive and
interact with the game, supporting design decisions before
testing with real participants.
II. RELATED WORK
This section surveys key studies across adventure, educa-
tional, health, cancer-related, and puzzle-based serious games.
Classic adventure games such as the Monkey Island series,
developed with the SCUMM engine, use spatially organized
data structures to support temporally coherent narratives. As
shown in the source code analysis in [5], the division into
“rooms” enables dynamic storytelling. Indiana Jones and
the Fate of Atlantis expands this model through branching
storylines and decision-making mechanics. Other titles like
Broken Sword: The Shadow of the Templars, The Legend of
Kyrandia, and the Pok´emon series illustrate a range of narrative
and interaction models, from inventory-based exploration to
turn-based combat.
Serious games for education and health leverage interactiv-
ity to promote scientific engagement and medical training. is a
well-known example where players manipulate protein struc-
tures to assist real-world biochemical research. Mind Scan-
ners integrates psychiatric diagnosis and treatment mechanics
within a dystopian setting, challenging players to balance
ethical decision-making with time management. Several games
aim to educate players and train professionals in cancer-related
scenarios. CˆancerSM [6], [7] train oncologists in managing
breast cancer side effects through interactive decision-making.
Cancer Sucks [8] uses real patient experiences to promote
empathy, while CˆancerSP [9] simulates prostate cancer case
management.
That Dragon, Cancer [10] explores the emotional impact
of pediatric cancer through a deeply personal narrative. Addi-
tional titles include Alpha Beat Cancer, which gamifies cancer
education for children, and CancerST [11], which integrates
a virtual pet mechanic to teach thyroid cancer management.
Cancer: Now What? enhances clinical training with AI-driven
patient interactions [12].
Puzzle-based games also contribute relevant design in-
sights through their emphasis on spatial reasoning and log-
ical problem-solving. Titles such as Q*bert [13] and Fez
[14] incorporate perspective-shifting mechanics to create com-
plex spatial challenges. Unpacking and Tiny Room Stories:
Town Mystery use environmental storytelling, where object
placement reveals narrative elements. Games like There Is
No Game: Wrong Dimension [15] challenge conventional
gameplay through meta-puzzle design, while The Incredible
Machine [16] remains a classic example of physics-based logic
puzzles in educational contexts.
The insights gained from these studies inform the develop-
ment of CancerSB, a serious game focused on bone cancer
awareness, designed to educate players about treatment op-
tions through interactive gameplay. By combining interactive
challenges, resource management, and narrative exploration, it
balances educational content with engaging gameplay, aligning
with best practices from related works.
III. GAME DESIGN AND DEVELOPMENT
The development of CancerSB (Figure 1) was guided by
design choices aimed at maximizing player engagement and
educational impact. The game employs a point & click adven-
ture format, which facilitates an intuitive learning experience
while allowing for deeper exploration of medical content
related to bone cancer.
Fig. 1. Initial game menu.
A. Visual Style and Development Tools
The artistic direction of the game was originally designed
to balance medical education with an engaging and adventure-
oriented aesthetic. The design employs a palette of neutral and
cool shades, evoking a sense of both clinical precision and the
tension of battle. This choice not only warrants the gravity of
the subject matter but also enhances the overall atmosphere of
exploration and combat.
An important visual strategy in the game is the gradual
deterioration of affected regions, symbolized by ancient ruins.
These serve as a metaphor for disease progression—evoking
the decline of once-great civilizations to reflect the irreversible
impact of untreated cancer. This reinforces the urgency of
timely and effective treatment. Combined with adventure and
combat elements, the approach creates an engaging experience
that connects clinical education with interactive gameplay.
The game was developed in Unity for its flexibility and
cross-platform support, with Adobe Photoshop used to refine
visuals and ensure graphical consistency.
B. Interdisciplinary Collaboration
The game was developed by a team of designers and
developers, with medical professionals consulted to ensure
accurate representation of bone cancer. By combining narrative
mechanics, educational challenges, and meaningful choices, it
bridges health education with interactive engagement.
C. Narrative and Thematic Structure
The opening scene of the game unfolds as a close friend
reaches out to the player, revealing their bone cancer diag-
nosis through a text message on a cellphone, as shown in
Fig. 2. Three different means of transportation are randomly
introduced in the message, and each unique combination leads
to new adventures and challenges.

Fig. 2. Opening scene of the game.
To enhance immersion and educational value, the game
is structured as an adventure journey through three world
regions—Chile, Italy, and China—each symbolizing parts of
the human body affected by a specific type of bone can-
cer. Chondrosarcoma, represented by Chile, typically affects
adults over 40 and targets the pelvis, proximal femur, proxi-
mal humerus, ribs, scapula, and craniofacial bones. Ewing’s
Sarcoma, linked to Italy, is more common in children and ado-
lescents, primarily affecting the pelvis, femur, ribs, humerus,
and spine. Osteosarcoma, represented by China, occurs more
frequently in adolescents and young adults, often impacting the
distal femur, proximal tibia, and proximal humerus (shoulder)
[1]. This narrative structure metaphorically mirrors disease
progression, prompting players to make strategic treatment
decisions while learning about its physiological and clinical
aspects. Each cancer type is mapped to an iconic architectural
structure, transforming gameplay into a journey of discovery
and metaphor. This design approach deepens immersion and
serves as an educational tool, translating complex medical
content into symbolic, memorable visual experiences (Fig. 3).
Fig. 3. Architectural landmarks are mapped onto a human skeleton to illustrate
cancer-susceptible bone regions in the game.
Mini-tutorials introducing key aspects of bone cancer—such
as its characteristics, symptoms, and treatment strategies—are
delivered to the player through interactive elements embedded
within one of the five environments of each country. These
educational segments are visually represented by a symbolic
ticket featuring a yellow ribbon, a reference to the international
awareness color for bone cancer. This design choice integrates
learning moments organically into the gameplay experience,
reinforcing the educational goals of the serious game.
In Chile, a bone cancer type is represented through a land-
mark evoking the Andean landscape and national resilience,
emphasizing adaptability and creativity in facing adversity.
In Italy, the Colosseum symbolizes an aggressive cancer,
with fast-paced challenges reflecting the intensity and strength
required to confront it. In China, the Temple of Heaven
represents a more insidious progression, highlighting the need
for strategic thinking and precision in treatment. The design
choice emphasizes both the nation’s cultural heritage and its
spirit of innovation, creating a visually immersive environment
that enriches the gameplay experience.
In summary, by aligning each type of cancer with a dis-
tinctive architectural structure, the game crafts a narrative
that transcends traditional entertainment. This metaphorical
approach not only illustrates the progression and complexity
of bone tumors but also stimulates strategic thinking regarding
treatment, effectively bridging the gap between physiological
understanding and culturally significant, historical symbols.
D. Gameplay Mechanics and Challenges
Within the isometric game environment, players navigate
through intricately designed scenes representing each country
(in this work, Chile, Italy, and China). Figs. 4.a–c illustrate
this gameplay structure: each country comprises five inter-
connected environments, with a central hub serving as a key
transition point. This spatial layout not only reinforces the
thematic connection between the cultural elements and the
medical challenges but also provides a structured yet dynamic
map for exploration. Players must strategically traverse these
interconnected areas, with the central piece acting as a nexus
for accessing the peripheral regions, each harboring unique
puzzles, challenges, and boss encounters that correspond to
specific types of bone cancer. This design choice enhances the
immersive experience, requiring players to plan their route and
resource management carefully, much like the strategic con-
siderations necessary in real-world medical decision-making.
The core mechanics of the game focus on solving puz-
zles and strategic decision-making, effectively simulating the
multifaceted challenges involved in diagnosing and treating
bone cancer. Throughout the game, players collect various
items—each symbolizing diagnostic tools and treatment op-
tions—that must be judiciously deployed to navigate increas-
ingly complex scenarios. This design not only engages players
in an immersive narrative but also serves as a metaphorical
representation of the medical decision-making process. Key
mechanics, treatment strategies, and progressive difficulty are
detailed as follows:
• Key Mechanics: Players are tasked with diagnosing bone
cancer cases through interactive decision-making tools
that replicate real-world diagnostic procedures through
medical puzzles. These puzzles are designed to mirror the
step-by-step approach used in clinical settings, emphasiz-
ing the critical role of systematic analysis in determining
an accurate diagnosis.
• Treatment

and potential side effects. This mechanic encourages
a nuanced understanding of the trade-offs inherent
in medical decision-making, thereby highlighting the
complexity of treatment planning in oncology.
• Progressive Difficulty: As the game progresses, the
challenges become increasingly intricate, mirroring the
escalation of complexity often encountered in advanced
cancer care. This progressive difficulty demands a deeper
understanding of cancer biology and medical interven-
tions, pushing players to integrate learned knowledge
with strategic application.
Together, these mechanics contribute to an educational
framework that helps simulate real-world medical challenges.
By integrating interactive gameplay with educational content,
CancerSB offers a novel and engaging way to support under-
standing of bone cancer diagnosis and treatment.
Each region introduces a unique environment culminating
in a symbolic boss battle, designed to embody a specific
type of bone cancer through metaphor and gameplay. These
encounters go beyond obstacles—they are central to the narra-
tive, blending immersive storytelling with educational insight.
Players engage strategically with the distinct clinical features
of each cancer type in a meaningful, interactive way.
To support the design, detailed flow diagrams were created
(not shown here due to space constraints). These diagrams
map item collection, puzzle-solving, and progression logic
across each country’s level. Structured like directed graphs,
they highlight how gameplay decisions lead toward the final
objective: defeating a cancer-specific boss that reflects the
medical and symbolic complexity of the disease.
Chile – Chondrosarcoma: In the Chile level (Fig. 4.a),
the player begins in Environment 1, the central hub that
introduces core gameplay mechanics. Here, they meet a young
female NPC who requests a golden statue stolen from her
family, offering a ticket for the next journey in return. In
Environment 2 (upper left), the player encounters movable
statues that present a riddle. These can be shifted diagonally,
backward, and forward; solving the puzzle by placing them
correctly rewards the player with a spear, later used as a
surgical tool in the boss battle. Crabs in the same area move
diagonally and provide additional clues to help solve the
puzzle. In Environment 3 (lower right), the player meets
two monkey NPCs. One, wearing a wig, asks for a colored
ball and returns a wig—essential to completing the statue
puzzle. The other, hanging from a tree, asks for a banana
and gives the golden statue originally requested by the young
NPC. Environment 4 (upper right) features a fruit puzzle
where players collect fruits and flowers to place in the correct
containers near an indigenous woman; completing this puzzle

unlocks the boss area. In Environment 5 (lower left), a toucan
NPC requests food without specifying the type. Through trial
and error, the player discovers that papaya is the correct item.
In return, the toucan provides narrative clues about the young
NPC’s importance and reveals that she can give the travel
ticket. Additionally, a yellow ticket resting on a stone offers
educational information about the region’s related bone cancer
and its treatment.
The Chile’s final boss represents the Chondrosarcoma as
a Mayan warrior (Fig. 5). This boss symbolizes the severity
and challenges faced by patients in treating this disease. The
correct use of the fighting strategies available to the player, as
well as the proper use of each tool, can lead to victory. The
boss is designed to attack with unpredictable, shifting patterns.
The battle requires players to think on their feet and adapt
to sudden changes in the boss’s behavior, mirroring the need
for innovative and flexible treatment strategies in managing
this type of cancer. The metaphor extends to the environment
itself, where the interplay between the modern structures and
the natural terrain represents the ongoing struggle between
traditional approaches and emerging medical innovations.
Fig. 5. Chondrosarcoma boss in Chile, affected region in brown.
The spatial layout of the five Environments is consistent
across all game worlds—Chile, Italy, and China. As such,
their relative positions will not be restated in the upcoming
descriptions.
Italy – Ewing’s Sarcoma: As in Chile, in the Italy setting the
gameplay unfolds across five interconnected environments. In
Environment 1, the player activates a fountain that fills nearby
bowls with water. During the animation, a diamond appears
at the top of the fountain, but it can only be collected once
all missions in the country are completed. In Environment
2, a lion and a soldier are locked in conflict. Feeding the
lion a chicken thigh calms it, unlocking access to Emperor
Caesar, who presents a quiz. A correct answer grants the
player three treatment potions: chemotherapy, radiotherapy,
and stem cell transplant. In Environment 3, a shepherd NPC
requests oil and salt to care for his sheep. Until these are
delivered, scene objects remain inactive. Fulfilling the request
unlocks additional interactions, including a yellow ticket in a
tree that offers educational content about Ewing’s Sarcoma. In
Environment 4, a senate man refuses to help the player unless
they bring the diamond from Environment 1. Once delivered,
he gives the player a sword, which becomes a surgical tool
in the final battle. In Environment 5, a girl NPC is seen
filling barrels with grapes. After finishing her task, she asks
for an extra barrel; in return, she offers the travel ticket. Wolf
NPCs also appear here, running diagonally when clicked. They
later request water, and if the player brings two bowls from
Environment 1, the wolves reveal a clue that ties back to the
shepherd in Environment 3.
The boss battle against Ewing’s Sarcoma takes place in
a Colosseum-inspired arena, where the final boss—a mino-
taur—symbolizes the threat of the disease. This boss (Fig.
6) combines brute strength with agility, requiring players to
alternate between offensive and defensive tactics across multi-
ple phases, reflecting the complexity of real-world treatment.
The historical setting reinforces the enduring fight against
aggressive cancers.
Fig. 6. Ewing’s Sarcoma boss in Italy, affected region in brown.
China – Osteosarcoma: As in the other regions, in the China
setting (Fig. 4.c) the player begins in Environment 1, where
core mechanics are introduced through a Lucky Cat quiz.
Correct answers grant radiotherapy (blue potion) and two
key collectibles for upcoming missions. In Environment 2,
a lake with cherry blossoms hosts a young NPC requesting
a fortune cookie, alongside a note about Osteosarcoma that
reinforces the educational theme. Environment 3 presents
a bamboo garden with a panda NPC and a yin-yang pond,
symbolizing well-being. The panda gives bamboo and, after
receiving a fortune cookie, rewards the player with a golden
key to unlock the boss area. A yin-yang object also reveals a
puzzle that, when solved, grants chemotherapy (pink potion).
In Environment 4, a temple serves as the final cinematic
setting. Here, the player delivers collected items and gains
access to the boss’s dojo—unlocked only with the golden
key after completing all missions. Two symbolic swords,
representing surgery, can be collected. Environment 5 features
a food stall where the player trades a collectible with an elderly
NPC for longevity noodles, completing a core side mission.
Upon fulfilling earlier tasks from Environment 2, the NPC
also provides immunotherapy (green potion). A medical kit
on a nearby table offers healing during the final battle.
The boss battle against Osteosarcoma takes place in front
of an iconic architectural landmark (Fig. 7). Personified as a
dragon, the boss mirrors the cancer’s aggressive nature—often

targeting the upper limbs—through rapid, unpredictable attack
patterns that demand quick and strategic responses. The en-
counter emphasizes precision, speed, and resource manage-
ment, symbolizing the urgency and complexity of treating
this disease. The interactive sequence adapts to both the
player’s decisions and the boss’s behavior, with attacks of
varying strength countered by defense, surgery, or item use.
This system reinforces the educational objective by simulating
the real-life challenges of combating Osteosarcoma through
strategic gameplay.
Fig. 7. Osteosarcoma boss in China, affected region in brown.
E. Template for Battle Scenes
A standardized base scene was developed as a template for
all boss battles in the game. It includes the essential scripts and
assets needed for each encounter and is subsequently adapted
for each country, with visual elements and gameplay logic
tailored to represent the characteristics of the corresponding
cancer type. Specifically, the battle follows an interactive se-
quence based on the player’s decisions and the boss’s actions:
• The battle begins with the boss launching an attack, which
may be weak, moderate, or strong.
• The player checks their remaining health:
– If depleted, the battle ends in a Game Over.
– If positive, the player can perform defensive or offen-
sive actions.
• The player’s actions include:
– Defend: A successful defense prevents damage and
restores energy.
– Attack (surgery): Reduces the boss’s health.
– Use backpack items: treatment potions (chemother-
apy, hormone therapy, and radiotherapy), healing items
(e.g., medications to recover health), and energy items
(e.g., food and water to restore energy).
• The boss continues attacking until its health is reduced to
zero, at which point the battle is won (cancer defeated).
• In Chile, unlike in the other countries presented (Italy
and China), treatment potions cannot be used during
the battle against Chondrosarcoma, reflecting realistic
treatment constraints, as this type of cancer is typically
resistant to conventional therapies such as chemotherapy
and radiotherapy.
IV. INITIAL VALIDATION USING SIMULATED USER
FEEDBACK
In developing our serious game, we investigate whether
ChatGPT 4o can effectively simulate survey responses, serving
as a proxy for real user feedback. Adapting the concept
of “mega-personas” [3], we prompt the model to reflect
diverse demographic profiles relevant to our target audiences.
This approach enables early-stage evaluation by generating
insights typically gathered from human participants, guiding
healthcare-focused game design. Our approach builds on prior
work with large language models [4], [17] and draws inspira-
tion from Steinmacher et al. [3] in simulating diverse human
demographics through the concept of “mega-personas”.
A. Methodology for Simulated UI and Gameplay Testing
This methodology presents a structured use of ChatGPT to
simulate user feedback for evaluating UI screens and gameplay
flow in serious game. By refining UX forms, customizing
prompts to detailed persona profiles, and analyzing the gener-
ated responses, it supports iterative design improvements. The
process begins with selecting key artifacts—UI screenshots
and gameplay diagrams, including menus, interfaces, dialogs,
and flowcharts. We adopt the “mega-personas” approach [3],
prompting the model to simulate feedback from well-defined
user profiles based on age, gender, cultural background,
gaming experience, familiarity with digital interfaces, and
healthcare-related interests, as follows:
• The Informed Patient: Aged 35–60; all genders; cultur-
ally diverse; often with direct or familial experience of
bone cancer. Gaming Experience: Limited, but motivated
to learn. Healthcare Interests: Seeks accurate, empathetic
representations of treatment and decision-making.
• The Curious Student: Aged 16–25; mixed gender and
cultural backgrounds. Gaming Experience: Moderate to
high; familiar with adventure games. Healthcare Inter-
ests: Values interactive learning and visual storytelling
on medical topics.
• The Healthcare Professional: Aged 25–65; medical
trainees or practitioners of varied profiles. Gaming Expe-
rience: Low, but comfortable with digital tools. Health-
care Interests: Prioritizes clinical accuracy and sees the
game as an educational and communicative resource.
• The Casual Gamer: Aged 18–40; diverse in gender and
culture. Gaming Experience: High; enjoys puzzles and
narratives. Healthcare Interests: Seeks entertainment with
optional educational value in an accessible format.
The goal of this strategy was to enable early evaluation and
inform design improvements before testing with users.
B. Prompt Template Design and Questionnaire
We created prompt templates instructing ChatGPT 4o to
simulate responses from the previously defined personas. To
ensure meaningful output, we focused on questions that are
objective and suited to scaled ratings. Each prompt included
descriptions of key visuals—such as opening scenes, game
home, and battle screens—as well as gameplay flow diagrams.

These inputs provided context for personas to assess overall
progression, challenge pacing, and task sequencing. Due to
space limitations, below are abbreviated examples of the
prompts used:
• Background information about the persona (e.g., “You
are a 45-year-old healthcare professional with moderate
experience in digital games...”).
• Context about the artifact under review (e.g., “Please
evaluate the following UI screen for a bone cancer serious
game. . . ”).
• A set of standardized survey questions—referred to as
the Simulated Persona Feedback Questionnaire—was
designed to evaluate key aspects such as aesthetics,
usability, ease of use, and gameplay flow. Participants
were prompted: “Please respond to the following survey
questions, providing ratings and comments based on your
profile”:

scene, and overall user interface (UI)? (1 = Non appealing, 5 = Strong
appealing)

C. Simulated Response Generation
For each artifact, we initiated a new ChatGPT conver-
sation using the custom prompt template. We ensured that
each conversation reseted the context, so the responses were
generated solely based on the provided persona profile and
artifact details. We asked each persona to respond to the survey
questions, simulating detailed feedback for each game scene
and gameplay flow.
D. Data Collection and Aggregation
We organized the data by survey question and persona,
and quantify the responses where possible (e.g., using Likert
scales) in a structured format (a CSV file). We extracted
numerical ratings and compute averages to gauge overall
feedback. We reviewed open-ended comments to capture re-
curring themes or unique suggestions that may inform design
adjustments. This aggregation was used to investigate insights
into common strengths and potential issues in the game’s
design, as perceived by the simulated user population.
E. Analysis and Validation
We explored variations across personas to observe whether
different demographic profiles perceived the UI or gameplay
differently. This simulated feedback offers preliminary insights
that support early-stage evaluation and can help inform later
user testing and design refinements in our serious game.
The UX questionnaire was designed based on established
evaluation instruments. Itens 1 and 2 were inspired by the
Curve [18] to assess visual attractiveness and overall aesthet-
ics. Itens 3 and 4 draw from the Post-Study System Usability
Questionnaire (PSSUQ) [19], focusing on interface usability
and clarity of in-game instructions, respectively. Item 5 is
based on the Game Experience Questionnaire (GEQ) [20],
targeting immersion and player engagement. Item 6 combines
insights from the Flow State Scale (FSS) [21], used to evaluate
challenge calibration and flow, and AttrakDiff [22], to assess
the clarity and perceived effectiveness of the educational
message. Item 7 was also inspired by visual perception com-
ponents in AttrakDiff. These references guided the design of
our questionnaire to balance usability, aesthetics, engagement,
and educational value.
V. SUMMARY OF SURVEY RESULTS ACROSS PERSONAS
The overall evaluation of the CancerSB across the Chile,
Italy, and China regions reveals consistently strong reception
across all four user personas. Median scores for each question
(Q1–Q6) considering all three countries scenarios show align-
ment in the game’s strengths: Visual Design (Q1) received
the highest scores (rate 5) from younger users (Casual Gamer
& Curious Student), while more mature personas appreciated
the design but noted the potential for added simplicity or
clarity, rating 4. Colors, Layout, and Typography (Q2) were
rated 5, highlighting excellent visual accessibility and thematic
coherence across all countries and personas. Navigation (Q3)
and Simplicity (Q4) consistently scored 4 across the board,
indicating intuitive design with slight room for enhancements
such as tutorials or visual cues. Gameplay Flow (Q5) and
Educational Puzzle Integration (Q6) were rated as logical
and engaging by all personas, with scores ranging from 4
to 5. The Student and Casual Gamer found the progression
especially fluid and interactive. Puzzle-solving elements were
also seen as effective in reinforcing educational messages
about bone cancer, particularly by the Informed Patient and
Healthcare Professional, who rated this aspect highest.
In addition to Q5 and Q6, simulated personas found the
Italy level the most challenging among the three gameplay
flows (Chile, Italy, China), likely due to its longer action
sequence, more NPC interactions, branching paths, and layered
puzzles. Chile and China were seen as more linear, with fewer
decision points and a more guided progression.
The visual game home design was generally well received
across persona, with ratings for overall appeal (Q1) ranging
from 3 to 4. The opening scene and UI were seen as clear
and engaging, particularly by users seeking empathetic and
informative content. While the Casual Gamer gave the lowest
scores (rate 3)—finding the visuals and UI somewhat simple
compared to commercial standards—the narrative style still
held potential appeal. For Q2 (colors, layout, and typography),
ratings ranged from 3 to 5, with all personas finding the design

appropriate for the health education context, especially the soft
tones, readable fonts, and consistent visual identity.
Battle scenes received high visual appeal ratings (4–5)
across all personas, with Student and Casual Gamer noting
their dynamic, immersive design. Colors, layout, and typog-
raphy were also well-rated (4–5), reflecting visual coherence.
Overall, game visuals—including opening, home, and battle
scenes—were consistently rated between 4 and 5.
The unified word cloud analysis (Q7) highlights “Educa-
tional,” “Cultural,” “Immersive,” and “Thoughtful” as the most
frequent descriptors (Fig. 8), reflecting a shared perception
across diverse profiles. The simulation indicates strong poten-
tial for the game to bridge entertainment and health education,
with users valuing its cultural sensitivity, visual clarity, and
interactive learning design.

VI. CONCLUSION AND FUTURE WORK
This study presented CancerSB, a serious adventure game
developed to promote bone cancer awareness and educa-
tion through culturally grounded, interactive gameplay. Using
a simulated user feedback approach based on the “mega-
personas” method, we conducted a preliminary validation of
the game’s visual design, gameplay flow, and educational
value. Results suggest that simulated personas provided mean-
ingful insights aligned with the target audience’s diverse
profiles. This strategy supported early-stage evaluation and can
guide future design refinements prior to real user testing.
As future work, we plan to conduct user studies with real
participants to further validate the game’s impact and usability.
We also intend to extend the game to include additional types
of bone cancer, new regions, mechanics, and progressively
layered challenges to enrich both gameplay and educational
content. Finally, future iterations will expand the game’s
educational reach to broader audiences.
